people.name: Honorius
people.summary: Younger son of Theodosius I, western emperor from age ten. His reign saw Stilicho's regency and execution, the Rhine crossing, the loss of Britain and the sack of Rome, which he watched from Ravenna.
people.detail: Passive and dependent on successive strongmen (Stilicho, Olympius, Constantius), he nevertheless survived seven usurpers. Procopius's tale of his pet chicken named Roma is a joke but captures his reputation. Married successively to Stilicho's daughters Maria and Thermantia, he left no children.

people.name: Arcadius
people.summary: Elder son of Theodosius I, eastern emperor 395-408, dominated in turn by Rufinus, the eunuch Eutropius, Gainas and his wife Aelia Eudoxia. His reign saw the Gothic crisis of 400 and the exile of John Chrysostom.

people.name: Theodosius II
people.summary: Eastern emperor for 48 years, the longest reign of any Roman emperor. Under him came the Theodosian Walls, the Theodosian Code, the councils of Ephesus (431 and 449), and the humiliating payments to Attila.
people.detail: Pious, scholarly ('the Calligrapher') and guided by his sister Pulcheria, the prefects Anthemius and Cyrus, and the eunuch Chrysaphius, he has been underrated; Millar's A Greek Roman Empire reconstructs a functioning, legally inventive government. He backed Cyril in 431 and Dioscorus in 449.
people.death: spinal injury after falling from his horse, 28 July 450
scholarship: Millar, A Greek Roman Empire: Power and Belief under Theodosius II (2006)

people.name: Constantius III
people.summary: Illyrian general who restored Ravenna's authority after 410: he crushed Constantine III, starved the Goths into returning Galla Placidia, married her, settled the Visigoths in Aquitaine and was briefly co-emperor. Father of Valentinian III.

people.name: Constantine III (usurper)

roles.t: Usurper in Britain, Gaul and Spain

people.summary: A common soldier proclaimed by the British army in 407, chosen, Orosius says, for his name. He held Gaul and Spain from Arles, was briefly recognised by Honorius in 409, and surrendered to Constantius in 411.
people.death: executed on the road to Ravenna, September 411

people.name: Priscus Attalus
people.summary: Ionian-born senator twice made emperor by the Goths, in 409-410 by Alaric and in 414-415 by Athaulf. Captured in 416, he was paraded in Honorius's triumph in Rome, had two fingers cut off, and was exiled to Lipari.

people.name: Joannes
people.summary: Senior civil servant proclaimed at Ravenna after Honorius's death in 423 and backed by Aetius. Defeated by Aspar's eastern army, he was mutilated, paraded on a donkey in the hippodrome at Aquileia and beheaded.

people.name: Valentinian III
people.summary: Son of Constantius III and Galla Placidia, emperor at six. His 30-year reign saw the loss of Africa, Attila's invasions and the dominance of Aetius, whom he murdered in 454; Aetius's men killed him six months later, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West.
people.death: assassinated on the Campus Martius, 16 March 455

people.name: Petronius Maximus
people.summary: Immensely rich senator, twice consul, who probably arranged Valentinian III's murder and seized the throne on 17 March 455. His 75-day reign ended as the Vandals approached Rome: fleeing, he was killed by the crowd or by soldiers.
people.death: killed in Rome while fleeing, 31 May 455

people.name: Avitus
people.summary: Arvernian aristocrat and friend of the Visigothic court who was made emperor in 455 with Theodoric II's support. Deposed by Ricimer and Majorian after the battle of Placentia, he was made bishop of Placentia and died soon after. Father-in-law of Sidonius Apollinaris.

people.name: Majorian
people.summary: Officer of Aetius, emperor 457-461 and the last western emperor to pursue a coherent programme of recovery: reforms against tax abuses, protection of Rome's monuments, campaigns restoring Gaul and an attempted invasion of Africa. When his fleet was destroyed in Spain, Ricimer had him beheaded.
people.death: executed by Ricimer's order near Dertona, 7 August 461

people.name: Libius Severus
people.summary: Lucanian senator installed by Ricimer after Majorian's execution, never recognised by Leo I, Aegidius in Gaul or Marcellinus in Dalmatia.
people.death: died at Rome, 14 November 465, perhaps poisoned (Cassiodorus)

people.name: Anthemius
people.summary: Eastern aristocrat, son-in-law of Marcian and grandson of the prefect Anthemius, sent by Leo I to rule the West in 467. He backed the great Vandal expedition and fought Euric, then fell out with his son-in-law Ricimer, who besieged and killed him in Rome.
people.death: beheaded by Gundobad in Rome, 11 July 472

people.name: Olybrius
people.summary: Anician senator married to Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III, and so Gaiseric's preferred candidate. Ricimer proclaimed him in April 472 during the siege of Rome. His daughter Anicia Juliana became Constantinople's greatest aristocratic patron.

people.name: Glycerius
people.summary: Gundobad's candidate, proclaimed at Ravenna on 3 March 473. Deposed without a fight by Julius Nepos in June 474, he was made bishop of Salona, where Nepos was murdered in 480, possibly at his instigation.

people.name: Julius Nepos
people.summary: Nephew of Marcellinus and ruler of Dalmatia, installed as western emperor by Leo I in 474. Driven out by Orestes in 475, he continued to claim the throne from Dalmatia and was recognised by Zeno and on Odoacer's coins until his murder.
people.death: murdered by his retainers near Salona, 9 May 480

people.name: Romulus Augustulus
people.summary: Teenage son of Orestes, proclaimed emperor on 31 October 475 and deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476; conventionally the last western Roman emperor. He was pensioned off with 6,000 solidi a year to the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples.
people.detail: His names, uniting Rome's founder and its first emperor, made him irresistible to later historians. He may have been the Romulus mentioned in a letter of Theodoric of 507-511 (Cassiodorus, Variae 3.35).

people.name: Marcian
people.summary: Thracian officer and protégé of Aspar, chosen by Pulcheria as husband and emperor in 450. He stopped tribute to Attila, convened the Council of Chalcedon, and left a full treasury, but refused to help the West or the Armenians.

people.name: Leo I
people.summary: Thracian or Dacian officer raised to the throne by Aspar in 457. He sent Anthemius and Julius Nepos to the West and launched the ruinous 468 expedition against Carthage, then murdered Aspar in 471 and built up Isaurian power through his son-in-law Zeno.

people.name: Zeno
people.fullName: Flavius Zeno (born Tarasis son of Kodisa)
people.summary: Isaurian chieftain who married Leo I's daughter Ariadne and became emperor in 474. Overthrown by Basiliscus in 475-476, he survived the revolt of Illus, issued the Henotikon, accepted the end of the western emperorship, and sent Theodoric to Italy.

people.name: Basiliscus
people.summary: Brother of the empress Verina, commander of the disastrous 468 expedition against the Vandals, and usurper in 475-476. His anti-Chalcedonian Encyclical alienated the capital; he surrendered to Zeno on a promise that his blood would not be shed and was starved to death instead.
people.death: starved to death with his family at Limnae, Cappadocia, 476/477

people.name: Anastasius I
people.summary: Palace usher from Dyrrachium chosen by the empress Ariadne in 491, whose financial reforms (abolition of the chrysargyron, the copper follis, tax collection by vindices, commutation of levies into gold) left a surplus of 320,000 lbs of gold. He won the Isaurian War, fought Persia (502-506), founded Dara and faced Vitalian's rebellion over his miaphysite sympathies.

people.name: Justin I
people.summary: Peasant from Bederiana near Naissus who walked to Constantinople as a youth, rose through the guards to command the excubitors, and was elected emperor in 518. A Chalcedonian, he ended the Acacian Schism. His nephew Justinian, whom he adopted, effectively ran his government.

people.name: Justinian I
people.summary: The great restorer of the sixth century: codified Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, rebuilt Hagia Sophia, reconquered Vandal Africa, Ostrogothic Italy and part of Spain, and fought Persia and the Balkan peoples, while surviving the Nika revolt and the plague.
people.detail: Born at Tauresium in Dardania, a native Latin speaker, he dominated his uncle Justin's reign and married the former actress Theodora in about 525, after Justin changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. Procopius gives three contradictory portraits. His religious policy aimed at reconciling the miaphysites while upholding Chalcedon, culminating in the Three Chapters controversy. His legacy is debated: an unsustainable overreach that exhausted the empire (the traditional view), or a reign whose costs were driven by plague and Persian aggression more than by ambition.
scholarship: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)

people.name: Justin II
people.summary: Justinian's nephew, who refused subsidies to the Avars and Persians, lost much of Italy to the Lombards (568) and provoked the Persian war of 572. The fall of Dara in 573 drove him insane; his wife Sophia and Tiberius governed for him.

people.name: Tiberius II Constantine
people.summary: Thracian officer, Caesar from 574 and emperor 578-582. Generous to the point of extravagance, he cut taxes and paid donatives, fought Persia with mixed success and lost Sirmium to the Avars. He chose Maurice as heir.

people.name: Maurice
people.summary: Cappadocian notary turned general and emperor. He restored Khosrow II and gained the favourable peace of 591, created the exarchates of Ravenna and Carthage, and fought a long and finally successful war against Avars and Slavs, but his economies with army pay provoked the mutiny of 602 that killed him.
people.detail: The Strategikon is attributed to him. His historian Theophylact Simocatta, writing under Heraclius, presents him as a pious ruler undone by parsimony. His fall is often seen as the true end of late antique stability in the East.
people.death: executed with five sons at Chalcedon by Phocas, 27 November 602
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)

people.name: Phocas
people.summary: Junior officer raised on a shield by the mutinous Danube army in 602. His reign of purges, conspiracies and military collapse before the Persians made him the archetype of the tyrant in Byzantine historiography; Heraclius overthrew him in 610.
people.death: beheaded and dismembered at Constantinople, 5 October 610
scholarship: Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)

people.name: Heraclius
people.summary: Son of the exarch of Africa, who overthrew Phocas in 610, lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to Persia, and then in the campaigns of 622-628 carried the war into Persia and destroyed Khosrow II. Within a decade of his triumph the Arabs took Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia and most of Egypt.
people.detail: He led his armies in person, the first emperor to do so since Theodosius I, and framed the war as a holy war for the True Cross. His father Heraclius the Elder had commanded at Solachon in 586. His second marriage, to his niece Martina, scandalised the church. His attempts at religious union (Monoenergism, the Ecthesis) failed. Kaegi's biography emphasises his skill and limits; Howard-Johnston his strategy and propaganda.
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)

people.name: Constantine III
people.summary: Heraclius's son by Fabia-Eudocia, co-emperor from infancy. He reigned with his half-brother Heraclonas for about three months after their father's death and died of tuberculosis, amid rumours that Martina had poisoned him.

people.name: Heraclonas
people.summary: Heraclius's son by Martina, co-emperor with Constantine III in 641 and briefly senior emperor under his mother's regency. Popular and military hostility forced the coronation of Constans II; late in 641 his nose was slit and he was exiled to Rhodes.

people.name: Galla Placidia
people.summary: Daughter of Theodosius I, captured at the sack of Rome in 410, wife of the Gothic king Athaulf, then of Constantius III, and regent of the West for her son Valentinian III. She played Bonifatius, Felix and Aetius against one another until Aetius prevailed.
people.detail: Her life traces the age: imperial princess, barbarian queen, Augusta, exile in Constantinople, regent. The so-called Mausoleum of Galla Placidia in Ravenna, with its starry blue mosaic vault, was probably built as an oratory of St Lawrence; she likely died and was buried at Rome.

people.name: Aelia Eudoxia
people.summary: Daughter of the Frankish general Bauto, married to Arcadius in 395 through Eutropius's scheming. Proclaimed Augusta in 400, she was a dominant figure at court and the enemy of John Chrysostom; mother of Theodosius II and Pulcheria.

people.name: Pulcheria
people.summary: Elder sister and guardian of Theodosius II, Augusta at fifteen, consecrated virgin and champion of the Theotokos. She probably helped bring down Nestorius, and in 450 married Marcian to legitimise his reign, presiding with him over Chalcedon.

people.name: Eudocia
people.summary: Daughter of an Athenian sophist, married to Theodosius II in 421. A poet (Homeric centos, a verse life of St Cyprian), she fell from favour around 441-443, reportedly over a suspected affair with the master of offices Paulinus, and spent her last years in Jerusalem as a patron of churches.

people.name: Licinia Eudoxia
people.summary: Daughter of Theodosius II, married to Valentinian III in 437. Forced to marry his murderer Petronius Maximus, she was carried off to Carthage by Gaiseric in 455 with her daughters and released in 462.

people.name: Honoria
people.summary: Sister of Valentinian III, whose letter and ring to Attila, after her affair with her steward and forced betrothal, gave Attila a pretext to claim half the West. Her fate after 450 is unknown.

people.name: Verina
people.summary: Wife of Leo I and sister of Basiliscus, an inveterate conspirator: she helped overthrow her son-in-law Zeno in 475, turned against Basiliscus, and in 484 crowned Leontius for Illus's rebellion.
people.death: natural causes during the siege of Papyrius, 484

people.name: Ariadne
people.summary: Daughter of Leo I, wife of Zeno and then of Anastasius I, whom she chose as emperor in 491. Her role as the bearer of dynastic legitimacy across three reigns made her the pivot of eastern politics for forty years.

people.name: Theodora
people.summary: Daughter of a bear-keeper of the Green faction and a former actress, married Justinian around 525 and was crowned with him in 527. Procopius credits her with saving the throne in the Nika riots; she protected the anti-Chalcedonians and was a powerful political partner.
people.detail: The Secret History's pornographic portrait of her youth is the most notorious piece of invective in Byzantine literature. Laws on women's property, actresses and forced prostitution have been linked to her influence. Her mosaic portrait in San Vitale is iconic. She is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches.

people.name: Sophia
people.summary: Theodora's niece and wife of Justin II, who governed during his madness, bought a truce from Persia in 574, and engineered Tiberius's elevation as Caesar. Later tradition blames her insult to Narses for the Lombard invasion.

people.name: Martina
people.summary: Heraclius's niece and second wife (married c. 613), who accompanied him on campaign and bore him at least nine children. Her attempt to rule for her son Heraclonas in 641 failed; her tongue was slit and she was exiled to Rhodes.

people.name: Amalasuntha
people.summary: Daughter of Theodoric, highly educated in Greek and Latin, regent for her son Athalaric. Opposed by Gothic nobles for giving him a Roman education, she negotiated secretly with Justinian, and her murder by her co-ruler Theodahad gave Justinian his casus belli.
people.death: strangled in her bath on Martana island, Lake Bolsena, 535

people.name: Serena
people.summary: Niece and adopted daughter of Theodosius I, wife of Stilicho and mother-in-law of Honorius. During Alaric's siege of Rome in 408 the Senate, suspecting her of collusion, had her strangled with Galla Placidia's assent. Zosimus says she had once taken a necklace from the statue of Rhea.
people.death: strangled at Rome by Senate decree, 408

people.name: Hypatia
people.summary: Mathematician, astronomer and Neoplatonist philosopher of Alexandria, daughter of the mathematician Theon, who edited commentaries on Ptolemy and Diophantus and taught pupils such as Synesius of Cyrene. She was murdered by a Christian mob in 415 during the feud between Bishop Cyril and the prefect Orestes.
people.death: murdered by a Christian mob in Alexandria, March 415
scholarship: Watts, Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher (2017)

people.name: Antonina
people.summary: Wife of Belisarius, daughter of a charioteer, and close ally of Theodora. She accompanied Belisarius on campaign, organised the deposition of Pope Silverius in 537, and helped Theodora bring down John the Cappadocian in 541. The Secret History portrays her adultery with her godson Theodosius in lurid detail.
